PMOS The Product Operating System

An operating system for product managers — where strategy, signal, and shipping live in one workspace.

After 10 years shipping enterprise products across regulatory SaaS, healthcare AI, and audit platforms, I kept rebuilding the same scaffolding by hand — PRDs in one tool, metrics in another, decisions buried in Slack. PMOS is the system I wish I'd had. It turns the messy, cross-tool reality of product work into a single, opinionated surface.

◎Vision
One surface for the entire product loop — from bet to outcome.

PMOS treats product management as a closed loop: form a thesis, define the bet, ship the increment, read the signal, decide what's next. Most teams stitch this loop across five disconnected tools. PMOS makes the loop the product — strategy docs, decision logs, roadmaps, and live metrics rendered as one continuous, queryable system rather than a folder of artifacts.

⚠Problem
PM work is fragmented across tools that don't talk to each other.

A modern PM context-switches across docs, trackers, dashboards, and chat — the same problem I solved for 15,000+ associates in a different domain. Strategy drifts from execution. Decisions lose their rationale the moment they leave the room. There's no system of record for why — only scattered records of what.

✦Why it matters
01
Decisions become assets
Every bet, trade-off, and reversal is captured with its reasoning intact — so the "why" survives re-orgs, hand-offs, and time.
02
Strategy stays connected
Roadmap items link upward to the thesis and downward to live metrics, so drift between intent and execution is visible immediately.
03
Built by a practitioner
Not a generic note-taking app with a PM template — an opinionated workflow shaped by a decade of shipping real enterprise products.

Highlight Reel

The Signal

Seven facts that tell you who I am as a PM — before you read a single case study.

01 — Biggest Platform
Regulatory platform live across EMA for 1,400+ Deloitte A&A practitioners — one of 5 products shipped across 3 companies over 10 years
Digital Tagging is the primary XBRL/iXBRL filing governance tool used by Deloitte's audit and assurance teams across EMA — not a prototype, not a pilot. The other 4 products span healthcare AI at Carelon and a utilization management platform at Cognizant.
02 — Sharpest Bet
Chose CoreFiling Beacon over building a custom XBRL engine in-house
The build-vs-buy decision saved an estimated 12–18 months of platform engineering while giving us best-in-class validation accuracy from day one.
03 — Most Surprising Insight
Auditors would abandon a tool if login took more than 90 seconds
Discovery interviews revealed that practitioners under deadline pressure equated slow authentication with product unreliability. This reframed RBAC from a security checkbox into a UX priority — driving Keycloak SSO to the top of the roadmap.
04 — Most Complex Stakeholder Environment
Aligned practitioners, legal, IT, and regional partners across 10+ EMA countries
No single market owner. Each country had different regulatory timelines, filing standards, and partner expectations. Shipped on schedule by ruthlessly scoping a common core and offloading localisation to a post-launch release.
05 — AI Product I Shipped
NLP assistant that unified prescription, claims, and HR data for 15,000+ Anthem associates
ACUBED A3 cut average query resolution time from multi-system manual lookups to a single conversational interface. First AI product I owned end-to-end — taught me where NLP confidence thresholds break trust.
06 — Failure I'm Proud Of
Shipped an ESG feature no one asked for and learned to kill scope sooner
Full story in the Scar Tissue section below. Short version: I mistook stakeholder enthusiasm in demos for validated demand. It wasn't. The module went live and went unused. Changed how I run discovery permanently.
07 — What I'm Building Toward
Enterprise software where regulatory complexity becomes a competitive moat
The most defensible SaaS isn't fastest or cheapest — it's the one that makes a hard compliance problem feel invisible. That's the product space I want to work in next.

🪡
Scar Tissue — The ESG Dashboard That Shipped and Went Unused
ESG Materiality Platform · Deloitte USI · 2022–2023
What Happened
Midway through the ESG Materiality Platform build, I scoped a benchmarking dashboard that let clients compare their materiality scores against industry peers. In discovery sessions and demos, stakeholders responded enthusiastically — "that would be really useful," "love that." I treated that as demand signal and built it into the sprint plan.

The feature shipped on schedule. Three months later, usage was near zero. When I went back to the same stakeholders, the honest answer was: they'd been polite in demos, not committed. No one actually owned the job of running peer benchmarks — it was interesting, not essential.
What I Changed
I now distinguish between enthusiasm and intent in every discovery session. Enthusiasm is easy to manufacture in a demo. Intent shows up when you ask "who would use this weekly and what would they do differently because of it?" — and get a specific, named answer.

I also introduced a lightweight commit test before any new feature enters scope: at least one named user agrees to be interviewed post-launch specifically about that feature. If no one will sign up for that conversation, the feature isn't ready to build.

The mistake cost one sprint. The framework it produced has saved several since.

AI Product Capabilities

Applying AI to Product

How I translate AI concepts into product decisions, user value, and business outcomes — as a product leader, not an implementer. The question is never "can we build it?" but "should we, for whom, and how do we measure it?"

💬
LLM Applications
Scope where a language model genuinely beats a deterministic feature — and where it doesn't. I frame LLM use cases around a clear job-to-be-done, define quality bars and guardrails before a line is written, and design the human-in-the-loop checkpoints that make output trustworthy enough to ship.
Use-Case ScopingQuality BarsHuman-in-the-Loop
🔗
Agentic Workflows
Decompose multi-step work into agent tasks with the right level of autonomy. I focus on where to keep a human in control, how to recover gracefully when a step fails, and how to prove an autonomous flow saves real time without quietly introducing new risk.
Task DecompositionAutonomy TradeoffsFailure Recovery

RAG Systems
Treat retrieval as a product problem, not just a pipeline. I prioritise which knowledge sources actually matter to users, set expectations for freshness and citation, and define how the product behaves when the answer simply isn't in the corpus — so confidence never outruns coverage.

Case Study · Carelon Global Solutions · Apr 2019–Feb 2021
ACUBED (A³) — AI Virtual Assistant
15k+Associates
AI/NLPTechnology
AnthemHealth Plan
Context & Problem

Anthem and Legato associates were context-switching across 4–5 internal systems to answer routine member questions. No unified interface. Average query resolution required multiple system logins — unacceptable latency when serving members in real time.

The Decision

The most contested product decision was defining a confidence-threshold policy: when the NLP model's confidence fell below a threshold, the assistant would surface a clear fallback rather than return a low-confidence answer. Stakeholders wanted 100% response coverage — every query answered, even uncertain ones. I pushed back. An incorrect answer delivered confidently destroys trust faster than a transparent "I'm not sure." The policy held.

Outcome

Shipped to 15,000+ associates across Anthem and Legato. Unified access to prescription data, claims, and HR knowledge. Resolution latency dropped measurably. Trust in the system held through launch because the fallback behaviour was honest about uncertainty.

Case Study · Cognizant · May 2016–Aug 2020 · Hyderabad
CareMore Utilization Management Platform
4 yrEngagement
COOLEngine Shipped
AnthemHealth Plan
Context & Problem

CareMore's care coordination teams had no systematic way to prioritise member outreach. High-risk members were missed; low-risk members received unnecessary calls. Outreach was entirely manual and coordinator-dependent.

The Decision

I designed COOL as a rule engine rather than an ML model. This was a deliberate choice: care coordinators needed to be able to explain to a supervisor — or a regulator — why a specific member was contacted on a specific day. A black-box model would have delivered better optimisation metrics but would have undermined coordinator trust and compliance auditability. Deterministic logic won on both counts.

Outcome

COOL engine shipped and adopted by CareMore care coordination teams. Systematic member outreach replaced ad-hoc processes across the 4-year engagement. Auditable logic allowed compliance teams to validate outreach decisions.
